title: “The Abbott roadshow is like some grotesque carnival of the worst elements of Australian political populism, turning the once great Liberal Party into the operating wing of Sky after dark.
text:
Article text size: This control adjusts article text size. For broader accessibility options, please use your browser or device text scaling settings.

As Liberal insiders confess they do not have the campaign infrastructure to match One Nation, Tony Abbott’s party leadership is being described as a return to the Credlin era.

Three days before Tony Abbott was elected unopposed as the Liberal Party’s federal president last month, his former chief of staff, Peta Credlin, took to social media, still in her workout wear. Beside her in a collar and tie stood Abbott.

After a campaign that had begun on Credlin’s nightly Sky News program, the pair celebrated their success in forcing Anthony Albanese to reverse a budget decision that had stripped funding from the parents of a deceased Victoria Cross winner.

“Thank you, Tony Abbott,” Credlin said, “because I know you made contact directly with the prime minister, and you wanted this fixed.”

A senior New South Wales Liberal insider says the post was noted by party operatives. Its meaning was taken to be deeper than the issue being discussed.

“It was a very cute – but also kind of curious – post that came out from Peta Credlin just days before Abbott got the presidency, which they knew was a foregone conclusion because he was running unopposed…

“Ostensibly they were saying, ‘Look what a great result this is that we won’, but what I thought they slightly misjudged was the optics. It was sort of like what they were really saying was, ‘We’ve put the band back together again.’ ”

Reflecting on Abbott’s prime ministership, the source says that having performed so magnificently in opposition, Abbott’s difficulty remains that he was then so terrible in government.

“While he will spend his life believing that he was cut down by the treachery of Malcolm Turnbull, he actually destroyed his own mandate by delegating his authority to Peta, to the extent that you even had Barnaby Joyce as deputy prime minister saying, ‘The problem with our government is that you can never get a decision in a conversation with the prime minister, because you always have to have a second conversation.’

“It created an ungainliness that radiated out from the prime minister’s office and just caused the permanent fracturing of relations with people who should have been his natural allies. We’re all obviously wildly speculating now about the future, but the Peta post, I thought, was a classic error of judgement – it indicated that the historical mojo will be unchanged. And inevitably, it invites the question: is this Tony and Peta’s party again?”

Another long-time observer of Abbott’s rise through the ranks of NSW Liberal Party politics describes Abbott’s basic formation as Jesuitical.

“At high school he absorbed, from various inspirational priests, the idea that one had a kind of destiny to do good, or at least to do something, so Tony is at his worst when he feels underutilised. The fuselage needs to be under strain for Tony to really feel like he’s a proper human being. There is nothing – nothing – he hates more than to be insufficiently utilised.”

To illustrate the point, the insider recalls Abbott’s days as a junior minister in the Howard government in the early 2000s, stomping around parliament like a bear with a sore head, often whingeing to MPs still languishing on the back bench about his own lack of promotion and venting his frustration at not being able to channel his Herculean energy.

“There are two schools of thought on Tony’s return to the Liberal Party presidency,” the Liberal insider says. “One is that he is there at the request of Angus, doing Angus a favour to try and add any kind of strength and momentum to the Liberal brand in its time of crisis and need.

“The other is that Tony is nursing a plan to return to the prime ministership, that having kind of seized the presidency of the party in a vacuum he will move to preselection in a lower house seat, and from there back to the leadership of a party that may have no other choices, and from there lead a magnificent rally of the Australian right that will carry him all the way back to the Lodge, in glory, like Napoleon out of exile from Elba.”

A third NSW Liberal, who has known and liked both Abbott and current leader Angus Taylor since their early days in politics, homes in on what he sees as the biggest problem with Abbott sitting in the president’s chair: the contrast that it immediately invites with Taylor.

“There’s no momentum in the Taylor caravan. He’s so obviously failed and I can’t see what he does that will ever turn things around. Compounding the problem is that Tony’s undisputed strength is from opposition. He is the greatest opposition leader in my lifetime,” the Liberal source says.

“And listen to him in the many media interviews he has given in recent weeks, and you can hear it, his ability to reduce an argument down to the three-word slogan, like ‘stop the boats’ or ‘cut the tax’, and now it’s ‘dump net zero’. And so listening to Tony almost becomes a bit of a study in contrast.

“The other is that Tony is nursing a plan to return to the prime ministership, that having kind of seized the presidency of the party in a vacuum he will move to preselection in a lower house seat … and from there lead a magnificent rally of the Australian right that will carry him all the way back to the Lodge, in glory, like Napoleon out of exile from Elba.”

“So that even to the extent that Tony is able to rally Liberals, and I think there is certainly a serious base of Liberal supporters who are Abbott lovers, the problem is that the more effective Tony is, there’s inevitably a kind of adverse distinction taking place with Angus, who has always been regarded as strong on policy and managerial skills but lacking retail cut-through.”

One senior Victorian Liberal, depressed at Abbott’s return to the national stage, recalls helping to build an “Abbott-proof fence” to keep Abbott out of Victoria, because nobody wanted to be photographed with him ahead of the 2014 state election. The source wonders whether Abbott has learnt anything in the time since.

“I think Tony actually loves Britain more, or at least as much, as Australia. He’s always sort of looked down his nose a little bit at the United States, but he’s all snapped heels and glassy eyed when looking to Britain, the monarchy and MI6.

“I think he’s conflicted. I don’t think he’s ever really got the idea of Australia as a Pacific power. If you wish to be a leader of a party of the future, you need to be able to distinguish between the gold and the dross, and Tony is still very much attached to the dross.”

Another Liberal, who sat at Abbott’s cabinet table and remains a deep admirer of the strength of his commitment to the Liberal cause, worries that Abbott’s presidency will forever be weighed down by the baggage he brings with him.

“Abbott’s desire to lead at the expense of anyone else has done more damage to the Liberal Party than any other single factor since 2007,” says this former minister. “He is single-handedly responsible for weaponising the climate change debate in the Liberal Party, which is at the heart of the never-ending cycle of leadership changes and dysfunction that has left the Liberal Party vulnerable to One Nation.”

Another former Liberal minister is even more pessimistic.

“He was so unpopular as a politician that the voters in his own electorate booted him out of a safe Liberal seat that has never turned back. I wonder how many other Liberal strongholds will have to fall for good to satisfy one failed politician’s ego,” the source says.

“The Abbott roadshow is like some grotesque carnival of the worst elements of Australian political populism, turning the once great Liberal Party into the operating wing of Sky after dark, where no minority is safe from a dog whistle, no bias or bigotry unwelcome, and decency is banished to a back cupboard to join the one or two remaining Liberal moderates shaking nervously in the dark.”

There are others who remember Abbott’s odd behavioural traits, like eating a raw onion during a visit to Charlton Farm Produce in northern Tasmania in 2015, or the 28 seconds of silent nodding that filled a 2011 television interview with Channel Seven political editor Mark Riley, after Abbott was asked to defend saying “sometimes shit happens” to military personnel mourning a killed soldier.

“He’s quite capable of walking right past you in a deserted city street and pretending that he’s so much in his own world that he hasn’t seen you,” one Liberal veteran says. “I know that because he’s done it to me. He’s a weird guy.”

Perhaps the biggest test of Abbott’s presidency will be how he handles the role should Taylor’s leadership face serious destabilisation in the wake of collapsing opinion polls. This week’s Newspoll had the Coalition’s vote at a paltry 18 per cent, 13 points behind the insurgent One Nation.

“The obvious – I would say, the only – contender sitting in the party room right now is Andrew Hastie,” a senior Liberal supporter of Hastie’s tells The Saturday Paper. “But Hastie and Abbott have fallen out very badly, so much so that a reconciliation is highly unlikely, if not impossible.

“What does Abbott do if the party room comes to the realisation that it simply cannot continue with Taylor as leader – a bit like when we dumped Abbott as leader?

“My fear is that he will do everything in his power to stop Hastie. And that could prove very destructive to the one very talented member of parliament that we have who is untainted by his attachment to past governments and is actually offering a fresh view of where we are headed.”

This week, Hastie used the yearly Tom Hughes Oration in Sydney to cast artificial intelligence as the era’s defining strategic threat, on a par with the Cold War nuclear race.

Describing a contest between five tech giants within the US, and a far more dangerous one between Washington and Beijing over Taiwan’s semiconductor dominance, Hastie warned that Australia risked repeating its abandonment of a sovereign nuclear deterrent under Menzies and Gorton by again becoming, in his words, a supplicant state.

“We must build a sovereign AI capability, or accept that Australia’s future will be shaped by other nations, a future with limited strategic options,” Hastie said. “Without sovereign AI, we will be a supplicant state tethered to the United States by submarine cables. I don’t want that. I’m a patriot and I want Australia to be strong, free, prosperous and secure.”

Ranging unusually wide for a shadow minister – Pope Leo XIV’s AI encyclical, Edmund Burke’s “little platoons”, Kai-Fu Lee on technological unemployment – Hastie emerged less as a free marketeer than an economic nationalist. He framed AI as continuous with old debates about nuclear sovereignty rather than culture wars. The impression was of someone auditioning for a seriousness beyond his current portfolio or his military past.

As a senior Liberal says: “The battle with Hastie is coming … and how Abbott handles it will be a big test for him.”

In the meantime, even Abbott’s detractors admit it is only with energy like his that the party can rebuild nationally.

The appointment of Lincoln Folo, a former federal director of the Liberal National Party in Queensland, as the Liberal Party’s federal director is widely seen as a step in the right direction.

“I think everyone has welcomed his appointment so warmly mainly because it wasn’t that fellow from Advance, Matthew Sheahan,” jokes one NSW Liberal.

“Still, he’s clearly a known quantity to Abbott and that’s important for the party to have a close relationship at that level. The other thing we know is that Abbott is very good at opposition.”

One NSW moderate who also recognises Abbott’s strengths as a campaigner nevertheless urged him to focus on rebuilding the party apparatus, which the source said was not anywhere near competitive with Labor’s machine or One Nation’s.

“I think probably the most important thing he could do – and I don’t know if he will, because he’s doesn’t really strike me as an organisational kind of guy – is to actually fix the fucking organisation. You know – the machinery and the fundraising and the staffing and the digital responsiveness and the stuff that, honestly, we are hopeless at. That’s what the job of a president actually is – and if he could do that, and just focus on that, then he might actually help us,” the source says.

“It struck me this last 10 days watching One Nation smash it with this ‘Fire the Liar’ fundraising campaign that supposedly raised $2 million or something and I was just struck at how quickly and professionally they kind of stood that thing up. They hopped onto a media story, they harnessed it, they weaponised it, they got the artwork done, they got the graphics done and they kind of surfed this thing beautifully, right?

“I mean, there’s no way the Liberal Party today could get an ad in the field that’s, like, responding to events and capitalising on them. That should have been us, right? That should have been the Liberal Party doing something like that, but we can’t. We’re just not organisationally capable of it. The machinery is too slow, the bureaucracy is too slow.

“So, my main message to Abbott is: stay out of the politics and fix the organisation, and, you know, run it, not all of us in Canberra.”

Jason Koutsoukis is The Saturday Paper’s special correspondent.
